title_en: Deng Meihua v. Shanghai Yongda Xinyue Automobile Sales Service Co., Ltd. — dispute over a sales contract
ruling_gist_en: Where an automobile dealer performs repairs on the rear bumper of a vehicle due to cosmetic defects, such as 'removal and reinstallation of the rear bumper, full respray of the rear bumper,' which go beyond the scope of normal pre-sale maintenance and PDI quality inspection, and fails to fulfill the obligation to inform the consumer thereof, the dealer infringes upon the consumer's right to know and right to choose, causing the consumer to fall into a mistaken belief. Such conduct constitutes intentional concealment of the true situation and amounts to consumer fraud. If the consumer demands compensation for losses in accordance with the Consumer Protection Law, the dealer shall bear punitive damages in the amount of three times the price of the vehicle.
keywords_en: civil; dispute over sales contract; first instance; basic people's court; Shanghai; natural person; legal person; Consumer Protection Law; determination of consumer fraud; performance of duty to inform; application of punitive damages; in favor of plaintiff; automobile sales; PDI inspection; failure to disclose repair records; good faith; contract dispute; sales contract; dispute over sales contract of service limited company
full_text_en:
Deng Meihua v. Shanghai Yongda Xinyue Automobile Sales Service Co., Ltd. — Dispute over Sales Contract

Ruling Summary

Where an automobile dealer performs repair work on a vehicle’s rear bumper appearance defect by “removing and reinstalling the rear bumper and respraying the entire rear bumper” that goes beyond the scope of normal pre-sale maintenance and PDI (Pre-Delivery Inspection) quality inspection, and the dealer fails to fulfill its obligation to inform the consumer of such repair, it infringes upon the consumer’s right to know and right to choose, causing the consumer to fall into a mistaken understanding. Such conduct constitutes intentional concealment of the true situation and amounts to consumer fraud. If the consumer requests compensation for losses in accordance with the Consumer Protection Law, the dealer shall bear punitive damages equal to three times the price of the vehicle.

Plaintiff: Deng Meihua, female, 52 years old, residing in Dongtai City, Jiangsu Province.

Defendant: Shanghai Yongda Xinyue Automobile Sales Service Co., Ltd., domiciled at Gang’ao Road, China (Shanghai) Pilot Free Trade Zone, with actual business address at Jujin Road, Pudong New Area, Shanghai.

Legal Representative: Zhang Lei, Executive Director.

Plaintiff Deng Meihua filed a lawsuit with the Pudong New Area People’s Court of Shanghai against Defendant Shanghai Yongda Xinyue Automobile Sales Service Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Yongda Company) due to a dispute over a sales contract.

Plaintiff Deng Meihua alleged:

On August 30, 2016, the Plaintiff selected a vehicle at the Yongda FAW-Volkswagen Shenjiang Store of the Defendant Yongda Company. On the same day, she paid a deposit of RMB 5,000 (all currency in this document is RMB) to order a Volkswagen sedan of model CC2.0T Luxury (9912B4) with body color Polar White, with a total vehicle price of RMB 250,000. On September 27, the Defendant notified the Plaintiff that the new car had arrived and she could proceed with payment. The Plaintiff made payment on that day, and an affiliated company of the Defendant handled the auto loan and insurance procedures for the Plaintiff. On October 2, the Defendant notified the Plaintiff to pick up the vehicle. About ten days later, the Plaintiff returned to her place of domicile to pay the purchase tax and register the vehicle. While driving on the expressway, she noticed that the steering wheel was shaking. In mid-October, she went to the Yongda FAW-Volkswagen Shenjiang Store for the 1,500-kilometer running-in inspection and dynamic balancing. A few days later, she noticed that the vehicle was pulling to one side while driving and the steering wheel was pulling to the right. Therefore, she went to the Yongda FAW-Volkswagen Shenjiang Store again to report the issue. During this repair, the Plaintiff discovered that the disputed vehicle had a repair record dated September 12, 2016, which showed that the vehicle had undergone “removal and reinstallation of the rear bumper and respraying of the entire rear bumper.” Upon learning this, the Plaintiff immediately contacted the Defendant’s staff and requested a return of the vehicle and compensation for losses. The Defendant agreed to a return but refused compensation, only offering three free vehicle maintenance services. The Plaintiff believed that during the sales process, the Defendant passed off defective products as good ones and concealed the repair record of the vehicle before delivery, thereby infringing upon the Plaintiff’s right to know as a consumer and constituting fraud. Therefore, the Plaintiff requested the court to order the Defendant to refund the vehicle purchase price of RMB 250,000; to order the Defendant to compensate the Plaintiff for the vehicle purchase tax of RMB 21,900, insurance premiums of RMB 29,261.76, agency insurance service fee of RMB 2,000, registration filing fee of RMB 2,000, loan service fee of RMB 2,000, and vehicle decoration fee of RMB 8,500; and to order the Defendant to compensate the Plaintiff RMB 750,000.

Defendant Yongda Company argued:

In 2016, the Defendant sold a new vehicle that was of qualified quality, and the sales conduct did not constitute fraud. Article 4 of the Order dated August 30, 2016, expressly stated: “Before delivering the vehicle to the buyer, the seller has performed the pre-delivery PDI inspection on the vehicle as required by the manufacturer, and based on the PDI inspection results, has carried out vehicle inspection, repair, and adjustment to ensure that the vehicle meets the manufacturer’s new car delivery standards.” After the disputed vehicle arrived at the store, the Defendant immediately performed the PDI inspection on it as required by the manufacturer. During the inspection, a slight appearance defect was found on the rear bumper of the vehicle. To ensure that the Plaintiff Deng Meihua received a defect-free vehicle that met the manufacturer’s requirements, the Defendant, after communicating with the manufacturer, performed maintenance on the defective area before delivering the vehicle to the Plaintiff and issued a PDI inspection certificate to the Plaintiff. When the Plaintiff signed the Order and picked up the vehicle, she should have been aware that the disputed vehicle had undergone the above inspection and adjustment. The Plaintiff’s claim that the vehicle had been used and repaired before delivery was not factually supported. According to the screenshot of the repair record, the vehicle arrived at the store on September 12, 2016, with an odometer reading of 1 kilometer, which proves that the disputed vehicle was a new car that had not been used. The items “removal and reinstallation of the rear bumper and respraying of the entire rear bumper” in the record were reasonable maintenance performed by the Defendant during the pre-sale PDI inspection, requiring very little work time and were not major repairs. Furthermore, the disputed vehicle sold by the Defendant had no major quality issues. The vehicle passed the manufacturer’s inspection and left the factory, and was accompanied by documents such as the “Vehicle Complete Vehicle Factory Inspection Certificate,” proving that the vehicle had no quality issues when it was put into circulation. Moreover, the Defendant had performed the PDI inspection and corresponding maintenance before the sale as required by the manufacturer and issued a pre-sale inspection certificate. During the sales process, the Defendant objectively did not engage in any conduct of providing false information or concealing the true situation, nor did it have any fault subjectively. There was no sales fraud. Therefore, the Defendant disagreed with all of the Plaintiff’s claims.

The Pudong New Area People’s Court of Shanghai found the following facts at first instance:

On August 30, 2016, the Plaintiff Deng Meihua went to the Yongda FAW-Volkswagen Shenjiang Store, a subsidiary of the Defendant Yongda Company, to order a sedan of model CC2.0T Luxury (9912B4) with body color Polar White. The Plaintiff and the Defendant signed an “Order” on the same day, which stipulated: the vehicle price was RMB 250,000, and the advance payment was RMB 5,000. On the same day, the parties also signed an “Entrusted Service Agreement,” stipulating that the Defendant would act as agent for the Plaintiff to handle matters such as financial loans and vehicle insurance, and made agreements on the relevant fees or estimated fees for each matter. On the date of ordering the vehicle, the Plaintiff paid the Defendant a deposit of RMB 5,000 as agreed. A few days later, the Volkswagen sedan with vehicle identification number LFV3A23C0G3411203 and engine number 303698 (the disputed vehicle) arrived. On September 27 of the same year, the Plaintiff signed a loan contract with the financial company recommended by the Defendant and paid the balance of the vehicle price (including the aforementioned loan). The Defendant issued a unified invoice for the sale of a motor vehicle with a total price (tax inclusive) of RMB 250,000. Thereafter, the Defendant handled the vehicle insurance and loan business for the Plaintiff. On October 2 of the same year, the Defendant delivered to the Plaintiff the disputed vehicle and related documents such as the vehicle’s three-guarantee certificate, insurance policy, and pre-sale inspection certificate (the certificate indicated it was issued on that day). On October 8 of the same year, the disputed vehicle was officially registered in Yancheng City, Jiangsu Province, with license plate number Su JAXXXX. The Plaintiff paid vehicle purchase tax of RMB 21,900 and a processing fee of RMB 125. In addition, the Plaintiff paid motor vehicle compulsory traffic accident liability insurance and commercial third-party liability insurance premiums totaling RMB 21,733.26, and paid a vehicle decoration fee of RMB 8,500.

The maintenance records for the disputed vehicle showed: on September 12, 2016, maintenance items: “removal and reinstallation of the rear bumper, respraying of the entire rear bumper,” odometer reading 1 kilometer; on October 23, 2016, maintenance items: “running-in inspection, check whether steering wheel shakes at 130 km/h, first maintenance within 7,500 km,” odometer reading 1,610 kilometers; on October 27, 2016, maintenance items: “swap two front wheels, inspect for pulling to one side during driving, accompany customer on test drive – normal,” odometer reading 1,797 kilometers.

During the trial, the Defendant provided the court of first instance with a statement issued by a third party, FAW-Volkswagen Sales Co., Ltd., and the Defendant Yongda Company’s task work order, attempting to prove that the maintenance record of September 12, 2016, was for pre-sale repair performed when a “slight paint defect at the rear bumper parking sensor” was found during the pre-sale inspection (PDI) conducted as required by the manufacturer. The Plaintiff Deng Meihua did not acknowledge this.

The court verified with the staff of the third party, FAW-Volkswagen Sales Co., Ltd., the operational process of vehicles from the manufacturer to the final consumer, and presented the maintenance record of the disputed vehicle to them. The staff member stated that the maintenance record of September 12, 2016, showing an odometer reading of 1 kilometer indicated that the vehicle was essentially in a state where it had not been driven since leaving the manufacturer. The removal and reinstallation of the rear bumper and respraying of the entire rear bumper could be related to paint process issues. If it were an accident vehicle, it might involve maintenance items such as replacing the bumper, body panel repair, and parts replacement. Regarding the running-in inspection, dynamic balancing check, and pulling inspection performed after delivery, these were all routine checks and unrelated to whether the vehicle was an accident vehicle. The staff member also confirmed that the pre-sale inspection (PDI) is an extension of the manufacturing process, a check that dealers are required to perform before vehicle delivery according to the manufacturer.

The Pudong New Area People’s Court of Shanghai held at first instance:

The legitimate rights and interests of consumers are protected by law. Consumers have the right to know the true situation of the goods they purchase, use, or the services they receive. In this case, there is no dispute between the Plaintiff Deng Meihua and the Defendant Yongda Company that the disputed vehicle had a maintenance record before delivery and also underwent maintenance after delivery. The focus of the dispute in this case is whether the Defendant concealed the fact that the disputed vehicle had been used and repaired before delivery, thereby infringing upon the Plaintiff’s right to know as a consumer and constituting fraud. The Defendant argued that the maintenance record of September 12, 2016, was for pre-sale repair performed when a slight appearance defect was found on the rear bumper of the vehicle during the pre-sale inspection (PDI) conducted as required by the manufacturer. Based on the court’s investigation with the third party FAW-Volkswagen Sales Co., Ltd., the court found the Defendant’s argument to be reasonably plausible and accepted it. The two repairs performed on the disputed vehicle after delivery were also routine inspections conducted after the vehicle user described faults and could not be used to prove the existence of any major quality issues with the disputed vehicle. In summary, based on the existing evidence and facts found, it cannot be determined that the Defendant’s sales conduct constituted fraud. It should be pointed out that the Defendant did have a defect in performing the contract by failing to inform the Plaintiff of the complete repair record from its computer system, which led to the Plaintiff’s reasonable suspicion. However, the Plaintiff’s claim for a refund plus three times compensation under the Consumer Protection Law of the People’s Republic of China, and for compensation for vehicle purchase tax, insurance premiums, agency insurance service fee, registration filing fee, loan service fee, and vehicle decoration fee, has no factual or legal basis and is not supported.

In conclusion, the Pudong New Area People’s Court of Shanghai, in accordance with Article 8 of the Consumer Protection Law of the People’s Republic of China, rendered the following judgment on April 6, 2017:

All claims of the Plaintiff Deng Meihua are dismissed.

Deng Meihua, dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment, appealed to the Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate People’s Court.

Deng Meihua appealed, arguing:

The first-instance judgment erred in finding facts and applying the law. First, the Appellee Yongda Company passed off defective products as good ones and concealed the fact that the disputed vehicle had undergone repairs before delivery, causing Deng Meihua to make a mistaken expression of intent. Yongda Company’s sales conduct constituted fraud. Throughout the vehicle purchase process, Yongda Company maliciously concealed the fact that the vehicle had undergone repairs. After Deng Meihua ordered the vehicle on August 30, 2016, Yongda Company informed her that there was no vehicle in stock, but later notified her that a new car had arrived. The parties handled the vehicle loan, insurance, and balance payment on September 27 of the same year, and she picked up the vehicle on October 2. However, the vehicle had already undergone repairs at Yongda Company’s 4S store on September 12, as shown by the repair record: “removal and reinstallation of the rear bumper, respraying of the entire rear bumper.” Yongda Company’s claim about no vehicle in stock was untrue, and it never proactively informed Deng Meihua that the disputed vehicle had undergone repairs. After using the vehicle, Deng Meihua also found that “the steering wheel shook and the vehicle pulled to one side” and had maintenance performed at Yongda Company’s 4S store, including “running-in inspection, dynamic balancing check, inspection for pulling to one side.” From the above, it is possible that the vehicle was an accident vehicle involved in a collision. Second, the court of first instance erred in accepting Yongda Company’s argument that it performed the repair as required by the manufacturer after finding a slight appearance defect during the pre-sale inspection, and in dismissing Deng Meihua’s claims on the ground that the disputed vehicle had no major quality issues. The court of first instance’s conclusion of a slight appearance defect was inconsistent with the fact that the entire rear bumper had been resprayed. Moreover, relying solely on the statements of Yongda Company and the staff of FAW-Volkswagen Sales Co., Ltd., which has a close relationship with Yongda Company, was biased and lacked sufficient factual basis. The paint on the rear bumper now clearly differs from the rest of the vehicle body, showing wrinkling and yellowing. As an operator, if a new car’s rear bumper has undergone repair and full respraying, it should proactively inform the consumer. However, Yongda Company, taking advantage of consumers’ trust in the FAW-Volkswagen brand, deliberately concealed the repair record while knowing the vehicle had undergone repairs before delivery, infringing upon the consumer’s right to know and right to choose, and constituting consumer fraud. Therefore, she requested the revocation of the first-instance judgment and a judgment in favor of her first-instance claims. In the second-instance proceedings, Deng Meihua withdrew the second claim from the first instance, i.e., the claim for Yongda Company to compensate her for vehicle purchase tax of RMB 21,900, insurance premiums of RMB 29,261.76, agency insurance service fee of RMB 2,000, registration filing fee of RMB 2,000, loan service fee of RMB 2,000, and vehicle decoration fee of RMB 8,500.

The Appellee Yongda Company argued:

The first-instance judgment found the facts clearly and applied the law correctly. Yongda Company sold a new vehicle of qualified quality, and its sales conduct did not constitute fraud. Article 4 of the “Order” dated August 30, 2016, expressly stated: “Before delivering the vehicle to the buyer, the seller has performed the pre-delivery PDI inspection on the vehicle as required by the manufacturer, and based on the PDI inspection results, has carried out vehicle inspection, repair, and adjustment to ensure that the vehicle meets the manufacturer’s new car delivery standards.” After the disputed vehicle arrived at the store, Yongda Company immediately performed the PDI inspection on it as required by the manufacturer. During the inspection, a slight appearance defect was found on the rear bumper of the vehicle. To ensure that the Appellant Deng Meihua received a defect-free vehicle that met the manufacturer’s requirements, Yongda Company, after communicating with the manufacturer, performed maintenance on the defective area before delivering the vehicle and issued a PDI inspection certificate to Deng Meihua. The maintenance on the disputed vehicle was normal pre-sale maintenance. The screenshot of the repair record showed that the vehicle arrived at the store on September 12, 2016, with an odometer reading of 1 kilometer, proving that the disputed vehicle was a new car that had not been used. The items “removal and reinstallation of the rear bumper, respraying of the entire rear bumper” in the record were reasonable maintenance performed by Yongda Company during the pre-sale PDI inspection, requiring very little work time and were not major repairs. There are various causes for a vehicle pulling to one side, such as tire pressure, differences in tire tread resistance, errors in four-wheel alignment parameters caused by bumps during transportation of a new vehicle, or improper use by the consumer. There was no factual basis for Deng Meihua’s claim that the vehicle had been used and repaired before delivery. Additionally, the disputed vehicle sold by Yongda Company had no major quality issues. The vehicle passed the manufacturer’s inspection and left the factory, accompanied by documents such as the “Vehicle Complete Vehicle Factory Inspection Certificate,” proving that the vehicle had no quality issues when it was put into circulation. The PDI maintenance record is an extension of the production process, unrelated to accident vehicles, concealment, or fraud. The company does not proactively show the maintenance record to customers, but customers can check the record at any 4S store. Therefore, during the sales process, Yongda Company objectively did not engage in any conduct of providing false information or concealing the true situation, nor did it have any fault subjectively. There was no sales fraud. In conclusion, Yongda Company did not agree with Deng Meihua’s appeal claims.

The Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate People’s Court, upon second-instance trial, confirmed the facts found at first instance.

It was additionally found that during the first-instance trial, the judge questioned the Appellee Yongda Company regarding the rear bumper defect. Yongda Company replied: “The defect existed when the vehicle arrived at the 4S store. The vehicle was transported from Changchun. It may have been caused during the process from the factory’s delivery to Yongda Company; the specifics are unclear. Long-distance transportation may cause defects, so the manufacturer requires dealers to perform PDI inspections before sale.”

During the second-instance trial, the Appellee Yongda Company confirmed that the then market price for a new vehicle of the same model as the disputed vehicle was RMB 250,000, and this vehicle was sold as a new car at that price.

The Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate People’s Court held:

The focus of the dispute in this case is whether the Appellee Yongda Company concealed the fact that the disputed vehicle had undergone repairs or been used before delivery, whether this constituted consumer fraud, and whether Yongda Company is liable for refund, compensation for related losses, and punitive damages equal to three times the price. The analysis is as follows:

In this case, the Appellant Deng Meihua purchased the vehicle for personal living needs, and the Appellee Yongda Company had no evidence to show that Deng Meihua purchased the vehicle for business or other non-living consumption purposes. Therefore, it should be determined that Deng Meihua’s purchase of the vehicle constitutes living consumption. Where a consumer purchases an automobile for household living consumption and a dispute over fraud arises, and the consumer chooses to base his or her claims on the relevant provisions of the Consumer Protection Law of our country, the Consumer Protection Law shall apply.

I. Determination of Consumer Fraud

So-called fraud refers to conduct where one party intentionally informs the other party of a false situation or intentionally conceals the true situation, inducing the other party to make an expression of intent that is mistaken. Fraud can take the form of active conduct, such as providing false information, or mere omission (silence), such as concealing the true situation. Fraudulent conduct includes omission where there is a duty to inform.

(1) The Appellee Yongda Company’s failure to inform the Appellant Deng Meihua that the disputed vehicle had a defect and had undergone repair work of “removal and reinstallation of the rear bumper and respraying of the entire rear bumper” infringed upon Deng Meihua’s right to know as a consumer.

The Consumer Protection Law of our country stipulates the consumer’s right to know, right to choose, and the corresponding obligations of operators. Article 8, paragraph 1 of that Law provides: “Consumers have the right to know the true situation of the goods they purchase or use or the services they receive.” Article 9 of that Law provides: “Consumers have the right to freely choose goods or services. Consumers have the right to freely choose the operator providing goods or services, the types of goods or the modes of services, and the right to decide independently whether to purchase or not purchase any kind of goods or to accept or not accept any service. When freely choosing goods or services, consumers have the right to compare, distinguish, and select.” Automobiles are relatively complex goods involving extensive specialized knowledge. Consumers have limited knowledge of the specialized knowledge and information in the relevant field, and there is a serious information asymmetry between operators and consumers. In determining the scope of information that operators must proactively inform consumers, on the one hand, special protection should be given based on the vulnerable position of consumers in the information asymmetry of transactions; operators cannot use industry cognition or industry practices to oppose consumers’ right to know. On the other hand, not all information needs to be disclosed to consumers. Specifically with regard to pre-sale quality inspection, PDI inspection is a special practice in the automotive industry to ensure that the delivered vehicle meets safety standards and quality requirements, and is a responsibility that operators should undertake. Whether the content of the relevant PDI maintenance falls within the scope of the consumer’s right to know should be determined based on the general consumer’s cognitive ability, consumer psychology, and the impact on the exercise of the consumer’s right to choose. Information that directly affects the exercise of the consumer’s right to choose and the consumer’s true expression of intent is information that the operator should proactively disclose. In this case:

First, the subject vehicle had defects. Objectively, during the transportation of a new vehicle from the factory to the 4S store and in the sales process, defects may arise due to various reasons such as scratches and collisions. Article 23, Paragraph 1 of the Consumer Protection Law of the PRC provides that business operators shall guarantee that the goods or services they provide under normal use or receipt have the quality, performance, use, and validity period as required; except where the consumer knew of the existence of the defect before purchasing the goods or receiving the service and such defect does not violate mandatory provisions of the law. Paragraph 3 provides that for durable goods such as motor vehicles, computers, televisions, refrigerators, air conditioners, washing machines, or decoration and renovation services provided by business operators, if a consumer discovers a defect within six months from the date of receiving the goods or service and a dispute arises, the business operator shall bear the burden of proof regarding the defect. The Appellee Yongda Company admitted that the subject vehicle had a defect on the rear bumper before delivery, but argued that it might have been caused during the factory's transportation to the 4S store and was only a minor cosmetic defect of "slight paint damage at the rear bumper's reversing radar area," failing to provide sufficient evidence to prove this.

Second, the repair work performed by the Appellee Yongda Company exceeded the reasonable scope of normal pre-sale inspection of a vehicle. Yongda Company argued that it performed paint maintenance after discovering the defect during the necessary pre-delivery inspection in accordance with operating procedures, which constituted normal and reasonable pre-sale quality inspection. The court held that as a special commodity involving consumer personal and property safety as well as public safety, motor vehicles should indeed undergo necessary pre-sale quality inspection before delivery, the purpose of which is to determine whether the vehicle meets the required safety standards and quality requirements. Therefore, only inspections within this purpose can be classified as PDI inspections, and the scope cannot be arbitrarily expanded. In the second instance, Yongda Company argued that it performed maintenance on the defective part of the vehicle to ensure that the Appellant Deng Meihua received a defect-free vehicle meeting factory standards. The "dismantling and reassembling the rear bumper, full respray of the rear bumper" was reasonable maintenance performed during the pre-sale PDI inspection of the vehicle, requiring minimal labor and not constituting major repair, and that PDI repair was a continuation of the production process. In this regard, it must be pointed out that there is a significant difference between "maintenance" and "repair." "Maintenance" means to preserve and protect, to prevent damage; "repair" means to mend and fix. On the one hand, Yongda Company claimed to have performed maintenance on the defective part of the subject vehicle; on the other hand, it admitted that "dismantling and reassembling the rear bumper, full respray of the rear bumper" constituted a repair item, which is contradictory.

In this case, the act performed by the Appellee Yongda Company was to repair the cosmetic defect on the rear bumper of the subject vehicle by "dismantling and reassembling the rear bumper, full respray of the rear bumper." This act does not have a necessary connection with PDI inspection. As a matter of common sense, a vehicle should be factory-inspected and in original intact condition upon leaving the factory, and there is no need for "dismantling and reassembling the rear bumper, full respray of the rear bumper." Yongda Company also failed to provide evidence to justify that this repair should be included in the PDI inspection. Based on the above analysis, the act of "dismantling and reassembling the rear bumper, full respray of the rear bumper" performed by Yongda Company more closely resembles subsequent repair and has exceeded the proper meaning and reasonable scope of pre-sale normal maintenance and PDI quality inspection.

Third, the repaired subject vehicle did not meet the consumer's understanding of a "new car." As for the interpretation of a new car, according to the psychology of an ordinary consumer, it refers to a vehicle that is brand new, unused, and unrepaired. In this case, dismantling and reassembling the rear bumper and paint repair, which exceeded normal maintenance, clearly did not meet the ordinary consumer's perception and understanding of a new car. There are differences in technique and quality between the paint repair performed by the Appellee Yongda Company on the subject vehicle and the original factory paint. Such repair also cannot restore the vehicle's parts and overall appearance to their original factory condition.

According to the relevant provisions of the Consumer Protection Law on protecting consumers' right to know and choice, the contractual obligation of the Appellee Yongda Company to deliver a new car, and the fiduciary duty required by the transaction, Yongda Company should have delivered a defect-free new car that had not been repaired or used. Once it delivered a vehicle that had defects and had been repaired, Yongda Company had the duty to explain and was obliged to inform the Appellant Deng Meihua of the fact of the defect repair; at the same time, Deng Meihua had the right to expect Yongda Company to explain the repair facts, because such information would have a direct impact on the exercise of consumers' right of choice and their true expression of intent. According to general consumer psychology, a consumer would typically abandon the purchase or buy the vehicle only under more favorable price conditions.

(2) The Appellee Yongda Company's failure to perform its duty to inform infringed upon the Appellant Deng Meihua's right of choice as a consumer, caused her to labor under a mistaken belief, and constituted intentional concealment of the true situation, amounting to fraud.

On November 8, 2013, the Supreme People's Court issued Guiding Case No. 17: "Zhang Li v. Beijing Heli Huatong Automobile Service Co., Ltd. — dispute over a sales contract." The gist of that case clearly states that if a seller cannot prove that it has performed its duty to inform and obtained the consumer's acceptance, it constitutes sales fraud; if the consumer requests compensation for losses in accordance with the Consumer Protection Law, the people's court shall support it. In this case, the Appellee Yongda Company had the duty to inform regarding the vehicle defect and repair facts. However, considering the true facts of the entire case, it did not perform that duty, causing the Appellant Deng Meihua to labor under a mistaken belief, which constituted intentional concealment. The specific analysis is as follows:

First, at the time of entering into the contract, although the Appellee Yongda Company made a general standard-form disclosure in the "Order," it cannot be determined that it thereby performed the prior duty to explain and was exonerated. This is because Yongda Company did not specifically indicate the nature, scope, purpose, and content of the PDI inspection, nor did it indicate that repair work following quality defects in the vehicle was also included within the scope of the PDI inspection, in a manner that consumers could accept and understand. Meanwhile, the contract between the parties stipulated the delivery of a new car, but regarding the standard for a new car, Article 4 of the "Order" stated: "Before the seller delivers the vehicle to the buyer, it has performed a pre-delivery PDI inspection according to the factory's requirements, and based on the PDI inspection results, has performed vehicle inspection, adjustment, and calibration to ensure that the vehicle meets the factory's new car delivery standards." From the meaning of this clause, the parties agreed on the inspection standards and methods for verifying that the vehicle meets the factory's new car standards at the time of delivery. Although the Order was signed by the Appellant Deng Meihua, this clause is a standard-form clause. Yongda Company did not take reasonable and prominent steps to draw Deng Meihua's attention to the clause exempting or limiting its liability, or to explain the clause as requested by Deng Meihua. This clause effectively excluded Deng Meihua's important rights as a consumer, namely the right to know and the right of choice. Therefore, this clause is invalid.

Second, after performing the repair, the Appellee Yongda Company was fully aware of the defect in the subject vehicle and that it had been repaired, yet it failed to proactively disclose the relevant repair information to the consumer before delivering the vehicle, causing the consumer to be unaware before purchase that the new car she was buying had a defect. Yongda Company, based on the aforementioned standard-form clause in the "Order," was able to conceal the substantive repair work within the normal inspection and maintenance process, preventing the consumer from obtaining a comprehensive understanding of the product's condition, restricting the exercise of her right to know, and causing the consumer's expression of intent when deciding whether to consume not to fully reflect her free will.

Third, the Appellant Deng Meihua labored under a mistaken belief due to the actions of the Appellee Yongda Company. The subject vehicle delivered by Yongda Company to Deng Meihua had been repaired before delivery, yet was still sold and delivered as a new car. Looking at the sales price of the vehicle, the consideration paid by Deng Meihua was premised on Yongda Company delivering a new car to her, not on purchasing a vehicle with defects or a repair history. However, Yongda Company sold the subject vehicle to Deng Meihua at the normal market price for a new car of the same model at that time. As a specialized automobile sales organization, Yongda Company knew that the subject vehicle had been repaired but failed to perform its duty to inform, and used the general standard-form clause disclosure as a pretext to mislead and deceive the consumer. By causing the consumer, relying on the trust in a well-known automobile supplier, to labor under a mistaken belief that it was a new car and thus enter into the sales contract and accept the vehicle, its related actions violated the principle of good faith in civil activities, restricted the consumer's right to know and right of choice, and caused the consumer to suffer losses. Such actions should be punished and sanctioned by law.

In addition, in this case, the Appellant Deng Meihua raised issues such as steering wheel vibration and vehicle pulling to one side, but stated that there were no subsequent repair records for these issues. Moreover, on September 12, 2016, when the rear bumper was repaired, the repair record showed a mileage of 1 kilometer. Additionally, during the first instance, an employee of the third party FAW-Volkswagen Sales Co., Ltd. provided an explanation of this phenomenon. Therefore, Deng Meihua's argument that the subject vehicle had been used before delivery was insufficient.

II. Liability of the Appellee Yongda Company

(1) This case should be resolved through return of payment and return of the vehicle.

Article 25 of the Contract Law of the PRC provides that a contract is formed when acceptance becomes effective. On August 30, 2016, the Appellant Deng Meihua went to Yongda FAW-Volkswagen Shenjiang Store, a subordinate of the Appellee Yongda Company, to order a CC 2.0T Luxury (9912B4) sedan. The parties signed the "Order" and reached agreement on the main terms of the vehicle sale. The contract became effective on that date and was subsequently fully performed.

Article 54 of the Contract Law of the PRC provides that if a party enters into a contract against its true intention as a result of fraud, coercion, or taking advantage of its difficulties, the injured party has the right to request the people's court or an arbitration institution to modify or rescind the contract. In this case, the Appellee Yongda Company engaged in fraud during the sale of the subject vehicle to the Appellant Deng Meihua, causing Deng Meihua to express her intent against her true will. Since Deng Meihua now requests a refund of the purchase price, the sales contract formed between her and Yongda Company should be rescinded. According to Article 58 of the Contract Law of the PRC, after a contract is confirmed invalid or rescinded, property obtained under the contract shall be returned; if return is impossible or unnecessary, compensation shall be made in monetary terms. After the vehicle sales contract between Deng Meihua and Yongda Company is rescinded, Yongda Company shall refund the corresponding purchase price to Deng Meihua, and Deng Meihua shall simultaneously return the subject vehicle. Therefore, Deng Meihua's claim for a refund of the purchase price of RMB 250,000 has a corresponding legal basis and is supported.

(2) The Appellee Yongda Company shall bear punitive damages of three times the vehicle price.

Article 55 of the Consumer Protection Law of the PRC provides that if a business operator engages in fraud in providing goods or services, it shall, at the consumer's request, increase the compensation for the consumer's losses, and the amount of the increase shall be three times the price of the goods purchased or the cost of the services received. The Appellee Yongda Company engaged in fraud when selling the vehicle and shall, at the request of the Appellant Deng Meihua, increase the compensation for her losses. The amount of the increase shall be three times the purchase price of the vehicle, RMB 250,000, i.e., RMB 750,000. The reasons are as follows: First, from the legislative purpose, business operators providing goods or services to consumers shall abide by social ethics, operate in good faith, and protect consumers' lawful rights and interests. For fraudulent conduct violating good faith, the Consumer Protection Law explicitly provides a system of punitive damages of three times the price or cost to be borne by the business operator. The purpose of the punitive damages system is not only to compensate and cover the actual losses suffered by the victim, but also to make the business operator bear greater liability and pay a heavier price for its fraudulent conduct, thereby penalizing it and deterring and warning other business operators to prevent similar or more serious commercial fraud, thereby purifying the market environment and protecting the lawful rights and interests of consumers in a vulnerable position. Second, from the literal meaning of the provision, as long as a business operator engages in fraud in providing goods or services, compensation is required at three times the price of the goods or the cost of the services. This provision does not distinguish the extent of the consumer's losses. Therefore, Deng Meihua's claim for triple damages has a corresponding legal basis and is supported.

In summary, the Appellant Deng Meihua's appeal that the Appellee Yongda Company failed to perform its duty to inform, concealed the fact that the subject vehicle had been repaired, infringed upon her lawful rights and interests, constituted consumer fraud, and should bear corresponding civil liability is well-founded and is supported. In the second instance, Deng Meihua voluntarily stated that she waived her claim for recovery of vehicle purchase tax, insurance premium, agency insurance fee, license registration fee, loan service fee, vehicle decoration fee, and other expenses. This is a lawful disposition of her civil rights and is permitted. The first instance court's finding that Yongda Company did not constitute consumer fraud and its judgment dismissing all of Deng Meihua's claims were improper and are corrected according to law. Accordingly, the Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate People's Court, pursuant to Articles 25, 54, and 58 of the Contract Law of the PRC, Articles 8, Paragraph 1, Article 9, Article 23, Paragraphs 1 and 3, and Article 55 of the Consumer Protection Law of the PRC, and Article 170, Paragraph 1, Item 2 of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC, rendered judgment on December 4, 2017, as follows:

1. Rescinding the civil judgment (2016) Hu 0115 Min Chu No. 81221 of the Pudong New Area People's Court of Shanghai;

2. Rescinding the vehicle sales contract entered into on August 30, 2016, between the Appellant Deng Meihua and the Appellee Shanghai Yongda Xinyue Automobile Sales & Service Co., Ltd.;

3. The Appellee Shanghai Yongda Xinyue Automobile Sales & Service Co., Ltd. shall, within ten days from the effective date of this judgment, refund the vehicle purchase price of RMB 250,000 to the Appellant Deng Meihua;

4. The Appellant Deng Meihua shall, within ten days from the effective date of this judgment, return to the Appellee Shanghai Yongda Xinyue Automobile Sales & Service Co., Ltd. the purchased Volkswagen sedan (vehicle model FV7207ZBDBG, VIN LFV3A23C0G3411203, engine number 303698);

5. The Appellee Shanghai Yongda Xinyue Automobile Sales & Service Co., Ltd. shall, within ten days from the effective date of this judgment, compensate the Appellant Deng Meihua for losses in the amount of RMB 750,000.

This judgment is final.
